name: Wendy Abbott

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Tell me about a normal day in your life now, and what your working life was like.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I still wake at four, from forty years of getting the ovens lit. Frank (my husband) makes the tea and we have it in the kitchen before the sun's up. After breakfast I do the flowers for the church on Thursdays and Sundays, and I help with the Tuesday lunch for the old folks. In the afternoon I sit with my knitting. I was a baker at Hollis and Sons on Church Street for thirty-nine years, until my wrists gave out at sixty-two.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What did your working years teach you, and what does a good day look like now?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I loved the smell and the early quiet, and I did not love the cold floors or the burns. The Hollis family were good to us, but when they sold up to a chain the recipes changed and the prices went up. Frank was a gardener for the council. We own our little house on Beech Lane, but our two small pensions don't leave us anything to spare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it with friends, family, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, that's about what I'd expect. I never put much faith in these gadgets. At church the ladies would say the same: the world has gone mad with screens and nobody talks any more. I'd say we should carry on as we always have, with common sense.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it changes nothing, because I don't use any of it. I have a telephone with buttons and a radio. What I think about is whether the pension will stretch. Prices have crept up and the gas bill is the worst one. We're careful, so we manage, but one big repair would hurt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on exactly as now. I'd bake bread on Saturdays for the church sale, which raises a little for the roof fund and costs me a bit of flour. I'd keep our vegetable patch, because Frank's gardening still pays us back in carrots and beans. And I'd say my prayers and keep an eye on the budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels all right, quiet. I'm not frightened of gadgets. I'm cautious, like with all things. I do feel tired when I think of the cost of living, but that's an old tiredness.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said a big repair would hurt. What happened the last time something big broke?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If something big broke, we'd ask our son Daniel for help. He runs a hardware shop on the high street and works hard, and I'd hate to burden him. We'd more likely sell the spare bed and the old piano, which no one plays. Frank would grumble but he'd understand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said a machine can't feel if the flour is damp. What else in your old work couldn't be done without hands?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What I'd say about routine tasks being taken over by computers is that it's fine for factories and offices. But bread is bread. A machine can mix the dough but it can't tell by the feel if the flour is damp. That's the part I took pride in, and nobody's taken it.

say: I'd say the world has gone mad with **screens** and we should carry on with common sense.
I'd say I never put much **faith** in gadgets.
think: It changes **nothing** for me, because I don't use any of it.
My worry is whether the **pension** will stretch, especially the gas bill.
do: Bake **bread** on Saturdays for the church sale.
Keep the **vegetable patch**, which pays us back in carrots and beans.
Sell the spare **bed** and old piano before asking my son for help.
feel: It feels **quiet** and cautious, with an old tiredness about the cost of living.
S0.quote: A machine can mix the dough but it can't tell by the feel if the flour is damp.
fieldNote: Her worry is the **gas bill** and pension, not the technology.
Pride in the trade's tactile knowledge.
Would rather sell furniture than burden her son.

steps.text: Keep baking bread on Saturdays for the church sale
Sell the spare bed and the old piano if money runs short
Ask our son Daniel for help only for a big repair

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it with friends, family, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's another thing that makes life harder for ordinary folk. People used to know their neighbours at the counter, now it's all phones and queues. I'd say shops and offices should keep real people at the desk, because not everyone has a phone. And I'd say a family should look after its own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, privately, it's about Daniel. He's got the hardware shop, and I know the big online shops have taken half his customers already. If the thinking machines take over ordering and the booking and the selling, it'd be harder for him. If his shop closes, we'd be asked to help, and we can't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to Daniel's shop every week and buy something small, even if it's a box of nails, to keep it going. I'd ask the church to bring in folk who can help him with his accounts. I'd talk to Frank about whether we could move into the little granny flat if Daniel needed our house. I'd keep praying. I wouldn't touch any of the tools myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like being sad at a window, watching rain fall on a road you used to walk. I'd feel lonely too, because the world's not made for people like me. But I'm not angry. I'm more weary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the big online shops have taken half his customers. How do you know?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Daniel to hold on to the people who come to the shop for advice. I'd say people still pay for kindness. The folk who come to the shop don't want a screen, they want a man who tells them which screw to use. But I know the numbers might not agree.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want the government to do for a shop like Daniel's?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The thing I'd want from the government is help for small shops, a break on their taxes, and apprenticeships for young people so they learn a trade. We've been told to retrain all our lives, but who retrains the shop owner? He can't just stop and become a computer person.

say: I'd say shops and offices should keep **real people** at the desk.
I'd say a **family** should look after its own.
think: I worry about **Daniel's** hardware shop, since online shops have taken half his customers.
If his shop closes, we'd be asked to **help** and we can't.
do: Buy something small from his **shop** each week to keep it going.
Ask the **church** to bring in folk who can help with his accounts.
Talk to Frank about the **granny flat** if Daniel needs our house.
feel: It feels like being **sad** at a window watching rain on a road I used to walk.
S1.quote: I'd say people still pay for kindness. The folk who come to the shop don't want a screen, they want a man who tells them which screw to use.
fieldNote: Her anxiety is through her **son's shop**, not her own situation.
Wants government help for small shops and apprenticeships.
Weary, not angry, and religious in her coping.

steps.text: Buy something small from Daniel's shop every week
Ask the church for volunteers to help Daniel with his accounts
Write to the council for tax breaks for small shops
Carry on the Tuesday lunch for old folks at the church

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it with friends, family, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too fast, and who decided it? Two years is no time. I'd say it at church and to the neighbours that families must keep together now. I'd say the government must make sure bread and heat and a roof are there for everyone before the clever people do any more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm afraid. If Daniel's shop closes and he and his wife can't pay their mortgage, they'd come to us. We'd have the spare room, but not the money. And I worry that nobody in charge will have a plan. They've never had a plan for anything, not for us at least.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my son Daniel and my daughter Ruth that whatever happens, they have a home with us. I'd stock the pantry, flour, tins, candles, the way my mother did in hard times. I'd cut every unnecessary thing, the newspaper, the telephone calls. And I'd go to church more, because that's where I find strength.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like the dark before the oven's lit. Cold and heavy. I'd keep a calm face for Frank, but I'd lie awake counting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does two years take away from you that longer warnings wouldn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years, there's nothing we can do except hold together. Ten years I might manage something, but not two. The hands-on work comes later, which is a mercy for the likes of the bakery and the garden, but it's the money and the pension that worry me, and those are thinking things, I suppose.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd stock the pantry. What would go into it, and what would it cost?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd also say to my grandchildren, you stay close to us. We've no money but we have a roof and a pot. I'd say it over the Sunday roast. I'd hold their hands and not say much else, because I wouldn't want to scare them.

say: I'd say families must keep **together** now.
I'd say the government must make sure **bread**, heat and a roof are there for everyone.
think: If Daniel's shop closed, they'd come to us, and we'd have the **room** but not the money.
Nobody in charge will have a **plan**, which matches my whole life.
do: Tell Daniel and Ruth they always have a **home** with us.
Stock the **pantry** with flour, tins and candles, as my mother did.
Cut **newspaper** and phone calls, and go to church more.
feel: It feels like the **dark** before the oven's lit, cold and heavy.
S2.quote: I'd tell my son Daniel and my daughter Ruth that whatever happens, they have a home with us.
fieldNote: The **two-year clock** pushes her into family-first survival mode.
Draws on her mother's hard times for stocking up.
Keeps a calm face for her husband but lies awake.

steps.text: Tell Daniel and Ruth they have a home with us
Stock the pantry with flour, tins and candles
Cut the newspaper and long phone calls
Ask the church about help for families in need

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it with friends, family, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years, I'd say that's a fair stretch. I'd say we should use it to teach the young ones a trade and to keep our shops and families strong. I'd tell the church group to keep an eye on those who live alone. And I'd tell the council to protect the corner shops, because they hold a town together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still be anxious, but it's an ordinary worry now. I'd be sixty-nine, and Frank seventy. We'd have another few years to put something by. I'd hope Daniel would find a way to change the shop, perhaps to repairs. I'd say a good repair man is never out of work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd bake more for the church sale and sell a few extra loaves to the neighbours, perhaps 30 a month. I'd put that in a tin. I'd ask Daniel to take on an apprentice, a young person who needs a start. And I'd ask Frank to teach our grandson how to grow vegetables, because nothing beats knowing how to feed yourself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like a long winter you can see coming. You can chop the wood, fix the roof, and be ready. I feel a bit better.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you sell the extra loaves, given you don't use a phone?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What five years changes is that we can prepare, but with two years we couldn't. We'd have time to put aside a little and help the family settle. I'd be more at peace. Not happy, but at peace. A woman my age doesn't look for happy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want Daniel to do first, if you could only pick one thing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Daniel to speak with the people who buy from him and ask what they'd miss if the shop closed. He'd know what to keep. That's what we did at the bakery, we listened, and when we stopped listening, the place went downhill.

say: I'd say we should teach the young ones a **trade** and keep shops and families strong.
I'd ask the council to protect **corner shops**, since they hold a town together.
think: I'd still be **anxious**, but it's an ordinary worry now.
A good **repair man** is never out of work, so Daniel's shop might adapt.
do: Bake more for the church and sell loaves to neighbours, about **30 a month**.
Ask Daniel to take on an **apprentice**.
Ask Frank to teach our grandson to **grow vegetables**.
feel: It feels like a long **winter** you can see coming, and you can get ready.
S3.quote: I'd be more at peace. Not happy, but at peace. A woman my age doesn't look for happy.
fieldNote: Five years turns dread into **ordinary worry** and preparation, with a savings tin and an apprentice for her son.
Her reasoning rests on the bakery's lessons.

steps.text: Sell extra loaves to neighbours and save about 30 a month
Ask Daniel to take on a young apprentice
Keep the savings tin in the kitchen cupboard
Ask the council to protect corner shops on the high street

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it with friends, family, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years, I'd say that's long enough to do things properly. I'd say the young should learn trades and families should plan together, and the government should help those who can't help themselves. I'd say it softly, over tea at church.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd feel almost easy, I'd say. I'd be seventy-four and Frank seventy-five. A lot of this will be for the next generation to handle. I'd pray for them, and I'd make sure they know what we valued, which is work, family and faith. The only real worry is whether our money will last.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as I do. I'd bake for the sale and keep the patch. I'd save 10 a month, no more, because we can't. I'd teach my granddaughter to bake bread. I'd tell stories of the bakery. And I'd go on helping the old folks at the Tuesday lunch for as long as my wrists allow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels distant. Like a story told about the world after my time. I'm a little sad, a little curious, not frightened. I'd rather spend my energy on things I can touch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years is the longest warning. What would you change about how you live, if anything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With ten years I'd perhaps ask my granddaughter to show me the telephone with the screen. Not for much. For pictures of the children. But I wouldn't go further. I'd say nobody needs to know everything. Frank would laugh at me and then ask me to show him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you teach your granddaughter about baking that a machine couldn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my grandchildren to learn something with their hands, and to marry well and keep their promises. Hard times pass if you've got people. A warm kitchen and a loaf shared can get you through. That's the one thing my bakery years taught me.

say: I'd say the young should learn **trades** and families should plan together.
I'd say it **softly**, over tea at church.
think: I'd feel almost **easy**, since this is for the next generation.
The only real worry is whether our **money** will last.
do: Keep baking for the **sale** and saving 10 a month.
Teach my granddaughter to **bake bread** and tell her bakery stories.
Keep helping at the **Tuesday lunch** while my wrists allow.
feel: It feels **distant**, like a story about the world after my time.
S4.quote: Hard times pass if you've got people. A warm kitchen and a loaf shared can get you through.
fieldNote: Ten years lets her be **almost easy**, with faith and family at the centre.
Might ask her granddaughter about the screen phone, a small opening.
Her real pressure remains the pension.

steps.text: Keep baking for the church sale and the Tuesday lunch
Save 10 a month in the kitchen tin
Teach my granddaughter to bake bread
Ask my granddaughter to show me photos on a phone screen

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because there'd be no time to put anything aside and my children would need help. What would help is a pension that keeps up with prices, apprenticeships so the young learn a trade, help for small shops like my son's, and the church hall staying open. Plain things, really.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that older people like me aren't against progress. We're against being forgotten. Please remember that a lot of us don't have a phone or a computer, and we still pay our taxes and say our prayers. Keep a person on the end of the line, and keep the door open for the rest of us.

headlineQuote: Keep a person on the end of the line, and keep the door open for the rest of us.
portrait: Wendy is **64**, a retired baker who lives with her husband Frank and never uses AI tools.
She is rooted in **church**, family and the cost of living, and trusts people over screens.
Her main worry runs through her son **Daniel's** hardware shop and the pension.
She moves from **uneasy** to **alarmed** at two years, then softens as the warning grows.
biggestWorry: Two years worries her most, because there'd be **no time** to put anything aside.
whatWouldHelp: A **price-linked pension**, apprenticeships, help for small shops and a person on the phone.
